A concrete Bloch Hamiltonian suitable for isolating the quantum-metric contribution is proposed:
$$
\mathcal{H}_0(\mathbf{k})=v\,\tau_x(k_x\sigma_x+k_y\sigma_y)+(m-bk^2)\tau_z+t k_x\tau_z,
$$
where $v,m,b,t$ are real parameters and $\boldsymbol{\sigma},\boldsymbol{\tau}$ are Pauli matrices acting in different orbital/spinor spaces. This Hamiltonian preserves combined $\mathcal{P}\mathcal{T}$ symmetry while breaking inversion $\mathcal{P}$, time reversal $\mathcal{T}$, and in-plane rotational symmetries when $t\neq 0$, thereby suppressing the Berry-curvature-dipole contribution and enabling the quantum-metric dipole $\Lambda_n^{ijk}$ to dominate the nonlinear Hall response. Numerical evaluation of $\Lambda_n^{xyy}(\mathbf{k})$ and the resulting nonlinear Hall conductivity $\sigma_{yx}^{\mathrm{qm}}$ (as functions of deformation parameter $t$ and Fermi energy $\varepsilon_F$) shows that (i) for $t=0$ the Fermi-surface distribution of $\Lambda_n^{xyy}$ is symmetric and $\sigma_{xyy}^{\mathrm{qm}}=0$, and (ii) increasing $t$ produces Fermi-surface asymmetry in $\Lambda_n^{xyy}$ and a nonzero $\sigma_{yx}^{\mathrm{qm}}$ whose magnitude grows with $t$. Model parameter values used in illustrations include $v=1\ \mathrm{eV\cdot nm}$, $m=0.1\ \mathrm{eV}$, and $b=1\ \mathrm{eV\cdot nm^2}$.

      $$
      \sigma_{ijk}^{\mathrm{qm}}=e^{3}\sum_n\int [d\mathbf{k}]\;\Lambda_n^{ijk}(\mathbf{k})\,f_0'(\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}),

Define the Berry curvature dipole (BCD) vector component $D_{ab}$ as $D_{ab} = \int \frac{d^n\mathbf{k}}{(2\pi)^n} \frac{\partial \Omega_{\mathbf{k}b}}{\partial \mathbf{k}_a} f_0(\mathbf{k})$, where $\Omega_{\mathbf{k}b}$ is the $b$-component of the Berry curvature at crystal momentum $\mathbf{k}$, $n$ is the system dimension, and $f_0(\mathbf{k})$ is the equilibrium Fermi-Dirac distribution; this relationship is the theoretical basis the authors use to connect band-structure Berry curvature to an intrinsic nonlinear Hall response.
[11]

State the modeling approach used to obtain quantitative BCD values: an eight-band tight-binding model for an Sb layer in the conventional unit cell is fit and optimized to reproduce density-functional theory (DFT) band structures near the Dirac point on the X-M line in the Brillouin zone; the model parameters are explicitly given as $\widetilde{m}_0=0$, $\widetilde{m}_1=0.48\,$eV, $t_0=0.97\,$eV, $t_1=1\,$eV, $t_2=-0.1\,$eV, $t_3=0.1\,$eV, $t_4=-0.04\,$eV, $t_5=0.145\,$eV, $t_6=-0.04\,$eV, and $\lambda_0=0.25\,$eV, and only the out-of-plane Berry curvature component $\Omega_{xy}$ is meaningful in the employed two-dimensional Sb-layer model; these modeling choices and parameters constitute the computational foundation for the predictive calculation.
[37]
Fig. 1

Explain the dimensional and symmetry approximations used as inputs to the calculation: the Fermi surface of BaMnSb₂ is nearly two-dimensional (2D), so the authors adopt a quasi-two-dimensional description (i.e. $n=2$ in the BCD integral); the antiferromagnetic order of Mn atoms is approximated as having negligible effect on energy bands near the Fermi surface, so time-reversal symmetry is approximated to hold in the calculations (this approximation is explicitly stated by the authors and used to justify the BCD computation).

Describe the band-structure features obtained from the fitted model: the model reproduces two gapped (massive) Dirac cones located near the X point and symmetrically placed at valleys denoted $K^{+}$ and $K^{-}$ (the two valleys are related by time-reversal symmetry), and these Dirac cones are spin-valley locked (spin projection is opposite in the two valleys), establishing the electronic structure from which Berry curvature hot spots arise.
Fig. 1
[37]

State the computed Berry curvature distribution: the out-of-plane Berry curvature component $\Omega_{xy}$ is large in the near-gap regime around each massive Dirac cone, and because Berry curvature is odd under time-reversal symmetry the two valleys ($K^{+}$ and $K^{-}$) host Berry curvature of opposite sign; this spatial distribution of $\Omega_{xy}$ supplies the local geometric ingredient for a nonzero BCD when asymmetry in momentum space is present.
Fig. 1(d)

Relate symmetry constraints to the BCD components: the calculated first partial derivatives $\partial\Omega/\partial k_x$ and $\partial\Omega/\partial k_y$ exhibit different symmetry properties—$\partial\Omega/\partial k_y$ is symmetric between the two Dirac cones and therefore can produce a nonzero net BCD along the $y$-direction (which corresponds to the crystallographic $b$-axis), whereas $\partial\Omega/\partial k_x$ is antisymmetric along both $k_x$ and $k_y$ due to the presence of the $M_b$ mirror plane (the vertical mirror plane parallel to the $b$-axis), so net BCD generated by shifts along $k_x$ is zero; from these symmetry properties the authors deduce the BCD is nonzero for Fermi-surface shifts (i.e., current-induced nonequilibrium occupations) along the X-M line (the $b$-axis) and vanishes for shifts along the orthogonal $a$-axis.
Fig. 1(e-f)

Report the quantitative energy dependence of the computed BCD (numerical results from the eight-band tight-binding model fitted to DFT): the BCD as a function of energy in the valence band becomes negative, reaching a minimum of approximately $-0.20\,$\AA; inside the bandgap the BCD is zero; in the conduction band the BCD is positive, rising sharply from the conduction-band minimum to a maximum of approximately $0.39\,$\AA at an energy $E_{\text{max}}\approx 23\,$meV above the conduction-band minimum; these numerical values are the principal quantitative predictions for the BCD energy dependence.
Fig. 4(a)

Conclude from the combined modeling, symmetry analysis, and numerical evaluation that BaMnSb₂, when described by the eight-band tight-binding model fit to DFT and treated as quasi-two-dimensional near the Fermi surface, hosts two massive spin-valley locked Dirac cones near the X point whose out-of-plane Berry curvature component is large and opposite in the two valleys; this yields a BCD that is nonzero along the X-M line (crystallographic $b$-axis current direction) but vanishes for Fermi-surface shifts along the orthogonal direction due to the remaining mirror symmetry $M_b$, with the calculated energy dependence showing a negative valence-band minimum of $\sim -0.20\,$\AA, a conduction-band maximum of $\sim 0.39\,$\AA at $E_{\text{max}}\approx 23\,$meV, and zero inside the gap.

motivating_questions.content: In order to establish whether a bulk, non-centrosymmetric Dirac material can produce an intrinsic NLHE at elevated temperatures, it is necessary to compute the geometric band quantities (Berry curvature and its momentum derivative) that determine the intrinsic contribution. Prior to this work, these quantities had been evaluated for selected 2D systems and for some Weyl semimetals, but not for a bulk, spin-valley locked Dirac material like BaMnSb₂ with its specific symmetry (space group Imm2), valley locations near X-M, and spin-orbit-induced Dirac gap. Without an explicit calculation one cannot (a) determine whether the two valley Berry curvatures produce a net BCD (because time reversal makes valley Berry curvatures opposite and crystal symmetries can either allow or cancel their derivatives), (b) quantify the energy scale and sign of the BCD as a function of chemical potential (necessary to predict temperature-dependent activation of NLHE), or (c) identify which crystallographic current directions (a-axis vs b-axis) should generate a finite intrinsic NLHE. These unanswered points prevented targeted experimental tests and device designs that exploit the BCD in BaMnSb₂.

The $m$-th order magnetic-field susceptibilities of band-resolved quantum-geometry tensors are defined as derivatives with respect to the magnetic field magnitude $B$ at $B\to0$: the Berry-curvature susceptibility is
      $$
      \alpha_{n}^{bc(m)}=\partial_{B}^{m}\Omega_{n}^{bc}=2\operatorname{Im}\!\left[\partial_{B}^{m}Q_{n}^{bc}\right]\big|_{B\to0},
      $$
      and the band-normalized quantum-metric susceptibility is
      $$
      \mathcal{G}_{n}^{bc(m)}=\partial_{B}^{m}\tilde{g}_{n}^{bc}=\operatorname{Re}\!\left[\partial_{B}^{m}\frac{Q_{n}^{bc}}{\varepsilon_{m}-\varepsilon_{n}}\right]\bigg|_{B\to0},
      $$
      where $n$, $m$ are band indices, $\varepsilon_{n}$, $\varepsilon_{m}$ are the band energies of the unperturbed Hamiltonian $H_{0}$, the quantum geometric tensor is $Q_{ab}^{n}=\operatorname{tr}\!\big(P^{n}\partial_{a}P^{n}\partial_{b}P^{n}\big)=g_{ab}^{n}-\tfrac{i}{2}\Omega_{ab}^{n}$, $P^{n}$ is the band projector of the total Hamiltonian $H=H_{0}+H_{B}$ (with $H_{B}$ the Zeeman term), $\tilde{g}_{n}^{bc}$ denotes the band-normalized quantum metric, $\Omega_{n}^{bc}$ is the Berry curvature of band $n$, and $g_{ab}^{n}$ is the quantum metric of band $n$.

$\kappa^{xy(m)}=\frac{e^{2}}{\hbar}\int\frac{d\mathbf{k}}{(2\pi)^{2}}\sum_{n}\big[\alpha_{n}^{xy(m)}f_{n}+(\partial_{B}^{m}f_{n})\Omega_{n}^{xy}\big]$,
where $\kappa^{xy(m)}$ is the coefficient of the $B^{m}$ term in the linear Hall conductivity expansion and $\partial_{B}^{m}f_{n}$ denotes the $m$-th derivative of the Fermi function with respect to $B$ evaluated at $B\to0$.

Relate the second-order nonlinear conductivity tensor to derivatives of Berry curvature and derivatives of the band-normalized quantum metric, thereby identifying two distinct physical contributions: the Berry-curvature-susceptibility-dipole (BCSD) contribution arising from the momentum derivatives of Berry-curvature susceptibilities and the band-normalized quantum-metric-susceptibility-dipole (QMSD) contribution arising from momentum derivatives of the band-normalized quantum-metric susceptibilities. Concretely, the general second-order expression written as
$\sigma^{ab;c}=\frac{e^{3}\tau}{\hbar^{2}}\sum_{n}\int_{\mathbf{k}}f_{n}\big(\partial_{k^{a}}\Omega_{n}^{bc}+\partial_{k^{b}}\Omega_{n}^{ac}\big)
-\frac{e^{3}}{\hbar}\sum_{n}\int_{\mathbf{k}}f_{n}\Big[2\partial_{k^{c}}\tilde{g}_{n}^{ab}-\frac{1}{2}\big(\partial_{k^{a}}\tilde{g}_{n}^{bc}+\partial_{k^{b}}\tilde{g}_{n}^{ac}\big)\Big]$
contains the BCSD in the terms proportional to derivatives of $\Omega$ (first line) and the QMSD in the terms proportional to derivatives of $\tilde{g}$ (second line).

Isolate the intrinsic second-order planar Hall and the intrinsic nonreciprocal longitudinal responses: the intrinsic second-order planar Hall conductivity receives contributions from both BCSD and QMSD (the BCSD part is weighted by the scattering time $\tau$ and involves momentum derivatives of Berry-curvature susceptibilities, while the QMSD part is intrinsic and independent of $\tau$), whereas the intrinsic nonreciprocal longitudinal second-order conductivity is governed solely by the QMSD contribution, as seen by the explicit intrinsic longitudinal expression
$\chi^{xx;x(1)}=-\frac{e^{3}}{\hbar}\sum_{n}\int_{k}\big(\partial_{k^{x}}G_{xx}^{n(1)}(\mathbf{k})\,f_{n}+\partial_{\mathbf{B}}f_{n}\,\tilde{g}_{x}^{n x}\big)$,
which contains only the first-order quantum-metric susceptibility $G^{(1)}$ and the band-normalized quantum metric $\tilde{g}$.

Summarize the symbolic mapping between susceptibilities and transport channels as follows: the linear planar Hall is produced by the Berry-curvature susceptibility $\alpha^{(m)}$ (plus occupation-derivative terms); the second-order transverse (planar Hall) conductivity contains BCSD $+$ QMSD contributions; and the intrinsic nonreciprocal longitudinal conductivity is produced solely by the QMSD. This constitutes the explicit assignment linking geometric susceptibilities to distinct magnetotransport channels.

motivating_questions.content: For experimental diagnosis and theoretical interpretation, it is crucial to know which microscopic geometric quantity controls each measurable transport response. Prior to this work, the symmetry constraints in altermagnets obscured which susceptibilities could be probed by which transport observable once a symmetry-breaking perturbation is applied. Without a clear assignment, experimental observations of magnetotransport could not be unambiguously attributed to Berry-curvature changes or to quantum-metric effects. Therefore a precise mapping from B-dependent geometric susceptibilities to linear and nonlinear conductivities is required to design experiments that selectively probe the Berry curvature versus the quantum metric in altermagnets.

steps.reasoning: Start from conclusion 2: the quantum metric $g_{\mu\nu}(\boldsymbol{k})$ is the intrinsic quadrupole of a wave packet, and the Berry curvature $\Omega_{\mu\nu}(\boldsymbol{k})$ governs the noncommutativity of the band-projected coordinates. These quantities are the building blocks of the semiclassical dynamics in a nonuniform electric field.

Within the adiabatic single-band approximation, the semiclassical equations of motion for a wave packet under a spatially varying electric field $\boldsymbol{E}(\boldsymbol{x})$ are:
        $$\dot{X}_\mu = \hbar^{-1} \frac{\partial\varepsilon}{\partial K_\mu} - \Omega_{\mu\nu} \dot{K}_\nu, \qquad \dot{K}_\mu = -e\left[E_\mu + \frac{1}{2} g_{\alpha\beta}(\boldsymbol{K}) \partial_\alpha\partial_\beta E_\mu\right],$$
        where $\varepsilon(\boldsymbol{k})$ is the band energy, $\boldsymbol{K}$ is the crystal momentum of the wave packet center, and $g_{\alpha\beta}(\boldsymbol{k})$ is the quantum metric.
        Lapa and Hughes, Phys. Rev. B 99, 121111 (2019); Kozii et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 126, 156602 (2021)

The term $\frac{1}{2}g_{\alpha\beta}(\boldsymbol{K})\partial_\alpha\partial_\beta E_\mu$ originates from the quantum metric and describes the effect of the electric field gradient on the crystal momentum dynamics.

For an insulating system where the chemical potential lies within the bulk band gap, the current response is obtained from these equations. Expanding in the wave vector $\boldsymbol{q}$ of the electric field, the quadratic order (the $q^2$ term) of the nonlocal Hall conductivity is:
        $$\sigma_H^{(2)}(\boldsymbol{q}) = \frac{e^2}{\hbar} \int_{\mathrm{BZ}} \frac{d^2\boldsymbol{k}}{4\pi^2} \frac{1}{2} g_{\alpha\beta}(\boldsymbol{k}) \Omega(\boldsymbol{k}) q_\alpha q_\beta,$$
        where $\Omega(\boldsymbol{k}) = \Omega_{xy}(\boldsymbol{k})$ is the scalar Berry curvature and $g_{\alpha\beta}(\boldsymbol{k})$ the quantum metric.

For the inversion-broken glide-protected Dirac semimetal the Berry curvature for band $n$ is given by
$$
\Omega_{n}(\mathbf{k}) = -\sum_{n'\neq n} 2\,\mathrm{Im}\frac{\langle u_n(\mathbf{k})|\nu_x|u_{n'}(\mathbf{k})\rangle\langle u_{n'}(\mathbf{k})|\nu_y|u_n(\mathbf{k})\rangle}{(\varepsilon_{n'\mathbf{k}}-\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}})^2},
$$
with velocity matrices $ \nu_\alpha=(1/\hbar)(\partial H/\partial k_\alpha) $. Time-reversal and glide symmetries impose the constraints
$$
\Omega_n(k_x,k_y) = -\Omega_n(-k_x,-k_y),\qquad
\Omega_n(k_x,k_y) = -\Omega_n(-k_x,k_y),
$$
and consequently
$$
\Omega_n(k_x,k_y) = \Omega_n(k_x,-k_y),
$$
so the Berry curvature is locally nonzero around each Dirac point and organizes into an anisotropic clover-type pattern consistent with these symmetry relations. The local separation of opposite-sign Berry curvature lobes in the Brillouin zone is identified as favorable for generating nonlinear Hall responses.

$$

$$
which the authors employ to compute $\Omega_n(\mathbf{k})$ for the bands of the tight-binding model.

Derive symmetry constraints on the Berry curvature from time-reversal $\mathcal{T}$: because time reversal maps $\mathbf{k}\mapsto-\mathbf{k}$ and sends $|u_n(\mathbf{k})\rangle$ to a Kramers-related state, the Berry curvature obeys the oddness relation
$$
\Omega_n(k_x,k_y) = -\Omega_n(-k_x,-k_y),
$$
which follows from the antiunitary nature of $\mathcal{T}$ and is the relation the authors state for the present time-reversal-symmetric system.

$$
as stated by the authors, reflecting that $\tilde{\mathcal{M}}_x$ reverses the sign of the Berry curvature with respect to $k_x$.

Combine $\tilde{\mathcal{M}}_x$ and $\mathcal{T}$ constraints to obtain mirror-even behavior in $k_y$: by composing the relations from time reversal and from $\tilde{\mathcal{M}}_x$ the authors deduce the constraint

      $$

Present the microscopic origin of the orbital coupling to an in-plane magnetic field in the tight-binding model: the magnetic field is implemented via Peierls phases obtained from the path integral of the vector potential $\mathbf{A}=z(B_{y},-B_{x})$ along hopping paths, so nearest-neighbour and interlayer hoppings acquire phase factors depending on $B_{x},B_{y}$; these phase factors enter the lattice structure functions $f_{1}(\mathbf{k})$ and $f_{2}(\mathbf{k})$ and hence the $4\times4$ Hamiltonian (the Hamiltonian matrix and the $f$-functions are written explicitly in the Hamiltonian block above). This implementation is purely orbital (no spin degrees of freedom or spin–orbit coupling are included in the Hamiltonian).

State that the planar magnetic field implemented through these Peierls phases breaks time-reversal symmetry at the level of the single-particle Hamiltonian because the Hamiltonian obeys $H^{*}(\mathbf{k})\neq H(-\mathbf{k})$ once the Peierls phases (which are odd under time reversal) are included; define time-reversal breaking here as failure of complex conjugation symmetry relating $H(\mathbf{k})$ and $H(-\mathbf{k})$. This broken time-reversal symmetry is the prerequisite for a nonzero Berry curvature distribution in the absence of spin–orbit coupling.

Combine the broken time-reversal statement with the expansion and parity constraints from conclusion 2 to conclude that a finite orbital magnetic-field coupling produces a nonzero Berry curvature $\Omega_{z}(\mathbf{k};B_{x},B_{y})$ (the expansion coefficients $a_{m,n}$ are generically nonzero when the Peierls phases are present) and therefore a finite BCD when integrated with the occupation derivative: because $a_{0,0}=0$ but coefficients with one exponent odd survive the symmetry cancellation, a nonzero in-plane field produces a nonzero first moment of $\Omega_{z}$ over occupied states.

$\vec{j}^{0}=\frac{e^{3}\tau}{2\hbar^{2}(1+i\omega\tau)}\hat{z}\times\vec{E}^{*}(\vec{D}\cdot\vec{E}),\quad
\vec{j}^{2\omega}=\frac{e^{3}\tau}{2\hbar^{2}(1+i\omega\tau)}\hat{z}\times\vec{E}(\vec{D}\cdot\vec{E}),$
where $e$ is the elementary charge, $\tau$ is the scattering time, $\omega$ is the drive angular frequency, and $\vec{D}$ is the Berry curvature dipole pseudovector defined above. motivating_questions.content: In the physical context of 2D electronic systems, demonstrations of Hall responses tied to band geometry have typically required either intrinsic inversion breaking with sizable spin–orbit coupling (producing Berry curvature hot spots and a nonzero BCD) or explicit magnetic order/Zeeman coupling. There was no established demonstration that the orbital effect of an in-plane magnetic field (which couples to electron motion via vector-potential induced hopping phases but does not involve spins) can alone generate the band Berry curvature textures whose first moment yields a BCD and hence a nonlinear Hall current. Without such a mechanism, theory could not predict QNLPE in nonmagnetic, spin–orbit–free 2D Dirac materials, nor could it propose magnetic-field control protocols for rectification/second-harmonic generation that do not rely on spin physics. Establishing an orbital-only route is therefore necessary to expand the class of systems and experimental setups that can realize quantum-geometric nonlinear responses.

A tight-binding supercell calculation of the KTaO3(111) 2DEG band structure (including quantum confinement and atomic SOC) yields multiple subband doublets with avoided crossings; the computed momentum-resolved out-of-plane Berry curvature $ \Omega_{z}(\mathbf{k}) $ exhibits pronounced hotspots near these avoided crossings, with typical peak magnitudes on the order of $2\times10^{3}\ \text{\AA}^{2}$. The Berry curvature distribution follows the threefold surface symmetry and changes sign as a function of energy, enabling a Berry-curvature triple. Within skew-scattering theory the nonlinear Hall conductivity scales as $ \sigma_{yxx}^{(2)} \propto \dfrac{e^{3}\tau^{3}}{p_{F}\tilde{\tau}} $, where $e$ is the electron charge, $ \tau $ is the symmetric scattering time, $ \tilde{\tau} $ is the skew-scattering time, and $ p_{F} $ is the Fermi momentum. The skew-scattering rate $ \tilde{\tau}^{-1} $ is proportional to the Berry-curvature triple
$ T(\epsilon_{F}) = 2\pi\hbar \int \dfrac{d^{2}k}{(2\pi)^{2}}\ \delta(\epsilon_{F}-\epsilon_{k})\,\Omega_{z}(\mathbf{k})\,\cos 3\theta_{k} $,
where $ \epsilon_{k} $ is the band energy and $ \theta_{k} $ is the polar angle on the Fermi surface. Using these inputs, the calculated $ \sigma_{yxx}^{(2)} $ reproduces the experimental gate-dependent peak–dip structure and sign changes, quantitatively reinforcing the skew-scattering interpretation and linking the observed NHE extrema to Berry-curvature hotspots near avoided band crossings.

steps.reasoning:
A tight-binding supercell model for the KTaO₃(111) 2DEG is constructed including quantum confinement along the KTaO₃ [111] direction and atomic spin–orbit coupling (SOC); the model reproduces known angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy results for the system and yields the multi-subband electronic structure used for Berry curvature calculations. 
[15]
Supporting Information S6

The calculated band structure from the tight-binding supercell shows multiple subband doublets with avoided crossings (anticrossings) produced by the combination of SOC, orbital hybridization among $d_{xy}$, $d_{xz}$, and $d_{yz}$ orbitals, and quantum confinement; these avoided crossings occur along high-symmetry directions (for example along the $\Gamma$–K direction) and are visible in the band dispersions obtained from the calculation. 
Fig. 5a, Fig. 5b, Fig. 5c

The momentum-resolved out-of-plane Berry curvature $\Omega_{z}(\mathbf{k})$ is computed from the tight-binding eigenstates for the relevant subbands; the Berry curvature displays pronounced localized maxima ("hotspots") in $k$-space that occur in the vicinity of the avoided band crossings, with typical peak magnitudes reported on the order of $2\times10^{3}\ \mathring{A}^{2}$ (two thousand square angstroms). 
Fig. 5d, Fig. 5e

The calculated Berry curvature distribution follows the threefold rotational symmetry of the KTaO₃(111) surface and exhibits sign changes as a function of energy (i.e., as the Fermi level crosses different regions), leading to a nonzero Berry-curvature triple appropriate to the $C_{3}$ surface symmetry; the threefold pattern and energy-dependent sign changes enable the definition of a Berry-curvature triple that weights $\Omega_{z}(\mathbf{k})$ on the Fermi surface with a $\cos 3\theta_{k}$ angular factor. 
Fig. 5d, Fig. 5e

Within skew-scattering theory, the nonlinear Hall conductivity is given parametrically by the scaling relation $ \sigma_{yxx}^{(2)} \propto \dfrac{e^{3}\tau^{3}}{p_{F}\tilde{\tau}} $, where $e$ is the electron charge, $\tau$ is the symmetric (momentum-relaxing) scattering time, $\tilde{\tau}$ is the skew-scattering time (the antisymmetric scattering time associated with a preferred scattering direction), and $p_{F}$ is the Fermi momentum; this relation indicates a cubic dependence on the symmetric scattering time and inverse proportionality to the skew-scattering rate. 
[22]

The skew-scattering rate $\tilde{\tau}^{-1}$ is proportional to the Berry-curvature triple on the Fermi surface, defined for the threefold system as 
$T(\epsilon_{F}) = 2\pi\hbar \int \dfrac{d^{2}k}{(2\pi)^{2}}\ \delta(\epsilon_{F}-\epsilon_{k})\,\Omega_{z}(\mathbf{k})\,\cos 3\theta_{k}$, 
where $\epsilon_{F}$ is the Fermi energy, $\epsilon_{k}$ is the band energy at momentum $\mathbf{k}$, $\Omega_{z}(\mathbf{k})$ is the out-of-plane Berry curvature at $\mathbf{k}$, $\theta_{k}$ is the polar angle on the Fermi surface, and $\delta(\ldots)$ is the Dirac delta function restricting the integral to the Fermi contour; thus $T(\epsilon_{F})$ quantifies the weighted Berry curvature on the Fermi surface that sources skew scattering in the threefold system. 
[22]
Fig. 5d–5f

Using the tight-binding Berry curvature distribution and the proportionality of the skew-scattering rate to the Berry-curvature triple $T(\epsilon_{F})$, the theoretical calculation evaluates $ \sigma_{yxx}^{(2)} $ as a function of Fermi level (or equivalently carrier density) and finds a gate-dependent variation with peak–dip structure and sign changes that reproduces the experimental gate-dependent nonlinear Hall conductivity qualitatively and quantitatively when fitting numerical coefficients (for example scattering times) to the experimental data. 
Fig. 5f

Because the Berry curvature hotspots lie near avoided band crossings and because $T(\epsilon_{F})$ changes sign when the Fermi level crosses regions where $\Omega_{z}(\mathbf{k})$ changes sign, the calculated $ \sigma_{yxx}^{(2)} $ links the experimentally observed gate-dependent extrema and sign changes in the nonlinear Hall response to Berry-curvature hotspots associated with avoided crossings in the computed band structure, thereby quantitatively reinforcing the skew-scattering interpretation and establishing a microscopic connection between band-structure Berry curvature and the measured NHE. 
Fig. 5d–5f

motivating_questions.content: To interpret gate-dependent nonlinear transport and to identify a microscopic origin for the observed NHE, a quantitative, momentum-resolved theoretical account of the band structure and Berry curvature in the confined KTaO3(111) 2DEG is required. Prior to this work there was no concrete calculation combining realistic tight-binding supercells (including multiorbital mixing and SOC) with explicit Berry-curvature evaluation and incorporation into a skew-scattering framework that provides (a) an estimate of hotspot magnitudes, (b) the energy dependence and sign changes of Berry curvature on the Fermi surface, and (c) a prediction of $ \sigma_{yxx}^{(2)} $ consistent with experimentally observed gate-dependent peaks and sign reversals. Without such calculations, the connection between measured nonlinear signals and specific band-structure features (avoided crossings, subband intersections) remained qualitative and unverified.

Starting from the tight-binding model (conclusion 6), the Berry curvature $\Omega(k)$ is calculated using the Kubo formula: $\Omega(k) = \sum_n f_n \Omega_n(k)$ with $\Omega_n(k) = -2\mathrm{Im} \sum_{m\neq n} \frac{\langle \Psi_{nk}|v_x|\Psi_{mk}\rangle\langle \Psi_{mk}|v_y|\Psi_{nk}\rangle\hbar^2}{(E_m - E_n)^2}$, where $f_n$ is the Fermi–Dirac distribution, $v_x = \frac{1}{\hbar}\frac{\partial H}{\partial k_x}$ and $v_y = \frac{1}{\hbar}\frac{\partial H}{\partial k_y}$ are velocity operators, and $|\Psi_{nk}\rangle$ are Bloch eigenstates.
                [56,57]

The Hamiltonian is parametrized using maximally localized Wannier functions constructed from the Pd $d_{xz}$ and $d_{yz}$ orbitals via the WANNIER90 package.
                [58,59]

The computed Berry curvature for the whole valence bands along high-symmetry directions (Fig. 5(b)) is nonzero and localized around the $K$ and $K'$ points, with the same sign at both valleys.
                Fig. 5(b)

The Chern number $C$ is obtained by integrating the Berry curvature over the first Brillouin zone: $C = \frac{1}{2\pi} \sum_n \int_{\mathrm{BZ}} d^2k \,\Omega_n(k)$. The integration gives $C = -1$, with each Dirac cone contributing $-0.5$.
Consequently, the anomalous Hall conductivity is $\sigma_{xy} = (e^2/h)C$, yielding a quantized Hall plateau of $e^2/h$ within the insulating gap of the spin-up Dirac cone.
Thus, PdCl₃ exhibits nontrivial Berry curvature and Chern number $C = -1$, implying a quantum anomalous Hall phase.

motivating_questions.content: The decisive topological question for PdCl$_3$ was not only whether spin-orbit coupling opens a gap, but whether the gapped phase is actually a Chern insulator with a nonzero bulk invariant. Before this calculation, the topological character of the PdCl$_3$ gap was unresolved, and without that information one could not claim quantum anomalous Hall behavior or predict quantized Hall transport.

motivating_questions.content: In crystals with a remaining mirror line the linear integral of the Berry curvature over occupied states is zero, so no linear dissipationless Hall conductivity arises. However, a spatially asymmetric distribution of Berry curvature on the Fermi surface can still have a nonzero first moment, the Berry curvature dipole. Prior to this work there was no explicit identification of how such a dipole, when induced by an in-plane Zeeman field in a two-dimensional trigonal crystal with strong spin–orbit coupling and inversion breaking, produces measurable second-order transverse currents at $\omega=0$ and $\omega=2\omega$; nor was there an explicit expression relating the dipole $D_{bd}$ to the nonlinear response tensor $\chi_{abc}$ in the presence of an AC driving field and finite scattering time. Because experiments can easily preserve a residual mirror line by orienting $\vec{B}$, the nonlinear APHE provides the only available Berry-curvature-based Hall signature in that symmetry sector, and making its quantum origin explicit requires both a microscopically consistent dipole definition and a formula for $\chi_{abc}$ that connects $\,D\,$ to observable currents.

For the low-energy two-band magnon model on a honeycomb ferromagnet near valley $\zeta=\pm1$, the Hamiltonian is $H_{\zeta}=h_0\sigma_0 + v_m(\zeta k_x\sigma_x + k_y\sigma_y) + \zeta\Delta\sigma_z$, where $\sigma_0,\sigma_x,\sigma_y,\sigma_z$ are Pauli matrices, $h_0$ is a constant energy shift, $v_m=3J_1S/2$ is the magnon velocity with $J_1$ the nearest-neighbor Heisenberg exchange and $S$ the spin magnitude, $\Delta=-3\sqrt{3}SD$ is the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI)-induced mass gap with $D$ the DMI strength, and $k_x,k_y$ are momenta measured from the valley point. The eigenenergy splitting is $\varepsilon_0 = \sqrt{v_m^2(k_x^2+k_y^2) + \Delta^2}$. Closed-form expressions for geometric quantities are:
      $$
      \Omega_{\alpha}^{xy}=-\frac{\alpha\Delta v_m^2}{2\varepsilon_0^3},\qquad
      \mathcal{G}_{\alpha,-\alpha}^{xx}=\frac{v_m^2(\Delta^2+k_y^2 v_m^2)}{4\varepsilon_0^4},\quad
      \mathcal{G}_{\alpha,-\alpha}^{xy}=-\frac{k_x k_y v_m^4}{4\varepsilon_0^4},\quad
      \mathcal{G}_{\alpha,-\alpha}^{yy}=\frac{v_m^2(\Delta^2+k_x^2 v_m^2)}{4\varepsilon_0^4},
      $$
      where $\alpha=\pm1$ labels the two magnon bands and $-\alpha$ denotes the opposite band. These analytic forms show that the quantum metric components scale as $\sim v_m^2/\varepsilon_0^2$ near band edges and the Berry curvature is proportional to $\Delta$.

There exists an intrinsic, scattering-time-independent nonlinear thermal current at second order in the temperature gradient $\nabla T$, arising solely from the band-resolved quantum metric. The intrinsic second-order energy current along spatial direction $a$ is
      $$
      J_a^{(2)}(\tau^0)=\frac{1}{\hbar}\sum_{n\ne p,\boldsymbol{k}}\frac{\varepsilon_n(\varepsilon_n+\varepsilon_p)}{\varepsilon_{np}}\Bigg[&\frac{f_n^B}{4\varepsilon_{np}}\big\{(\varepsilon_n^2-\varepsilon_p^2)\partial_a G_{np}^{bc}-G_{np}^{bc}\partial_a(\varepsilon_n^2-\varepsilon_p^2)\big\}\\
      &+G_{np}^{ac}\big(2\varepsilon_n\partial_b f_n^B+f_n^B\partial_b(\varepsilon_n+\varepsilon_p)\big)\Bigg]E_T^{b}E_T^{c},
      $$
      where $\varepsilon_{np}=\varepsilon_n-\varepsilon_p$, $f_n^B=(1-e^{\varepsilon_n/k_B T})^{-1}$ is the Bose-Einstein distribution with temperature $T$ and Boltzmann constant $k_B$, $E_T\equiv -\nabla T/T$ is the thermal field, $\partial_a\equiv\partial_{k_a}$, and the band-resolved quantum metric is $G_{np}^{bc}\equiv\mathrm{Re}[\mathcal{R}_{np}^b\mathcal{R}_{pn}^c]$, with $\mathcal{R}_{np}^a=i\langle u_n|\partial_{k_a}|u_p\rangle$ the Berry connection between bands $n$ and $p$ ($n\neq p$) and $|u_n\rangle$ Bloch eigenstates. The summation runs over bands $n\neq p$ and crystal momentum $\boldsymbol{k}$. This contribution is gauge invariant and independent of the relaxation time $\tau$.

The interband term in the second-order DC conductivity $\sigma_{\mathrm{DC}}^{\alpha;\beta\gamma}$ also yields a generalized Berry-curvature contribution $\sigma_{\mathrm{gBC}}^{\alpha;\beta\gamma}$ built from higher derivatives of Bloch states. Under the approximations $\mathrm{Im}f(\epsilon_n+i\eta)\simeq\eta(\partial f/\partial\omega)_{\epsilon_n}$ and $\epsilon_{nm}^2\tau^2\gg1$ (with $\eta$ constant imaginary self-energy, $\tau=1/(2\eta)$, $\epsilon_n$ eigenvalues of $\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{eff}}$, $\epsilon_{nm}=\epsilon_n-\epsilon_m$), this contribution decomposes into
$$
\sigma_{\mathrm{gBC}}^{\alpha;\beta\gamma}=\sigma_{\mathrm{gBC:re}}^{\alpha;\beta\gamma}+\sigma_{\mathrm{gBC:im}}^{\alpha;\beta\gamma}+\sigma_{\mathrm{gBC:add}}^{\alpha;\beta\gamma},
$$
where
$$
\sigma_{\mathrm{gBC:re}}^{\alpha;\beta\gamma}\simeq\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}\sum_{n,m(\neq n)}\frac{\Omega_{S';n,m}^{\alpha;\beta\gamma}}{\epsilon_{nm}\tau}\left(-\frac{\partial f}{\partial\omega}\right)_{\epsilon_n},
$$
$$
\sigma_{\mathrm{gBC:im}}^{\alpha;\beta\gamma}\simeq -\sum_{\boldsymbol{k},n}\frac{\Omega_{S';n}^{\alpha,\beta\gamma}}{\tau}\left(-\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial\omega^2}\right)_{\epsilon_n},
$$
and $\sigma_{\mathrm{gBC:add}}^{\alpha;\beta\gamma}$ is a multiband correction involving three-band processes (see paper for full expression). Under time-reversal symmetry, this generalized Berry-curvature term is the only contribution that can produce a nonzero nonreciprocal DC conductivity $\sigma^{\alpha;\alpha\alpha}$, but it requires finite dissipation ($\eta\neq0$) and—for two-band models—nonlinear momentum dependence in the Hamiltonian (e.g., quadratic $k^2$ terms) so that diagonal second derivatives $\mathcal{J}^{\alpha\alpha}=\langle\alpha|\partial^{\alpha\alpha}\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{eff}}|\alpha\rangle\neq0$ for the band state $|\alpha\rangle$.

The quantum contribution to the nonlinear anomalous planar Hall effect (APHE) resides in the antisymmetric dissipationless part of the nonlinear Hall conductivity vector χ_c = ε_{ab}χ_{abc}/2, where χ_{abc} is the second-order response tensor and ε_{ab} is the two-dimensional Levi-Civita symbol, while the semiclassical contribution occupies the symmetric part. This decomposition is established for time-reversal-invariant systems in Ref. [47] (Nandy and Sodemann, Phys. Rev. B 100, 195117 (2019)). This symmetry classification is assumed to carry over to the case where time-reversal is broken by the planar magnetic field, without providing a proof or symmetry analysis under magnetic field reversal.

premises.content: When the planar magnetic field is perpendicular to a mirror line of the trigonal crystal ($\alpha = 2\pi n/6$), the mirror symmetry $\mathcal{M}_x$ (which maps spatial coordinates $\{x,y\}$ to $\{-x,y\}$) forces the integral of the Berry curvature over the occupied Fermi surface to vanish, so the linear anomalous planar Hall effect (APHE) is zero. In this configuration, however, a finite Berry curvature dipole defined as $D_{bd} = \int_k f_0\,\partial_b \Omega_d$ still exists, where $f_0$ is the equilibrium Fermi-Dirac distribution and $\int_k$ denotes integration over the Brillouin zone. This dipole gives rise to a nonlinear anomalous planar Hall effect that appears at second order in an AC driving electric field $E_c = \mathrm{Re}(\mathcal{E}_c e^{i\omega t})$, generating transverse currents at zero frequency and at twice the driving frequency: $j_a^{0} = \chi_{abc} \mathcal{E}_b \mathcal{E}_c^*$ and $j_a^{2\omega} = \chi_{abc} \mathcal{E}_b \mathcal{E}_c$, where $\chi_{abc} = -\epsilon_{adc} e^3 \tau D_{bd} / [2(1+i\omega\tau)]$, with $e$ the elementary charge, $\epsilon_{adc}$ the Levi‑Civita tensor, and $\tau$ the scattering time.

steps.reasoning: The authors have derived that the nonlinear APHE arising from the Berry curvature dipole is described by the response tensor $\chi_{abc} = -\epsilon_{adc} e^3 \tau D_{bd} / [2(1+i\omega\tau)]$ (from conclusion 2).

They define the nonlinear Hall conductivity vector $\chi_c = \epsilon_{ab} \chi_{abc} / 2$, which extracts the antisymmetric (dissipationless) part of the second‑order response. The Berry curvature dipole contributes to this antisymmetric part.
[47]

The paper notes that in addition to this quantum contribution, there is a coexisting semiclassical second‑order contribution to the nonlinear Hall response that is independent of the Berry curvature phase. This semiclassical part resides in the symmetric part of the nonlinear Hall conductivity tensor.
[45]

Therefore, the Berry curvature dipole contribution can be isolated as the antisymmetric, quantum‑origin component of the nonlinear APHE. This allows experimental distinction: the quantum contribution is dissipationless and odd under magnetic‑field reversal, whereas the semiclassical contribution is symmetric and even.

motivating_questions.content: The nonlinear planar Hall effect discovered in the configuration where the linear APHE vanishes can have both a quantum origin (from the Berry curvature dipole) and a semiclassical origin (from conventional magnetoconductance anisotropy). To understand the underlying physics and to enable experiments to separate the two, it was necessary to identify which part of the nonlinear conductivity tensor carries the quantum contribution. In analogy with the time‑reversal‑symmetric nonlinear Hall effect, the Berry curvature dipole was expected to contribute to the antisymmetric dissipationless part, but this had not been demonstrated in the context of a planar magnetic field that breaks time‑reversal symmetry. Without this identification, one could not attribute the nonlinear Hall currents specifically to geometric properties of Bloch electrons.

The Berry curvature $\Omega(\mathbf{k})$ of the occupied electronic states (here $\Omega(\mathbf{k})$ denotes the Berry curvature as a function of crystal momentum $\mathbf{k}$ in the two-dimensional Brillouin zone) was computed from the SOC-included band structure (the Wannier Hamiltonian provides the matrix elements needed to evaluate Berry curvature); the Berry curvature distribution along high-symmetry paths and in the Brillouin-zone regions near the original Dirac points was examined.

The computed Berry curvature shows that the regions of $\mathbf{k}$-space surrounding the two Dirac points possess Berry curvature of opposite sign (i.e., one valley carries positive Berry curvature while the time-reversal-related partner valley carries negative Berry curvature). By time-reversal symmetry, these opposite signs correspond to opposite Berry phases accumulated around the two Dirac points.
Fig. 3(c)

Because the two valleys (the two Dirac-point regions) carry opposite Berry curvature/phase, the system exhibits valley-contrasting topological properties characteristic of a quantum valley Hall insulator: define a quantum valley Hall insulator as a system in which inequivalent valleys carry opposite valley Chern numbers or opposite Berry-phase contributions, enabling valley-dependent transport phenomena. The authors therefore classify the SOC-gapped monolayer as also being a quantum valley Hall insulator in addition to a $Z_{2}$ quantum spin Hall insulator.

conclusion.content: Model calculations for Bernal bilayer graphene were performed using an effective two-band Hamiltonian with parameters $v, v_3, v_4, \gamma_1$, a displacement field $u_D$, and a trigonal-warping/strain parameter $\delta$. The Hamiltonian describes low-energy electronic states in a single valley of bilayer graphene. Numerical evaluation of k-space integrals yields (i) a pronounced enhancement of both the density of states and either the Berry-curvature dipole or the quantum-metric dipole near the band-edge chemical potentials $\mu\approx\pm u_{D}/2$, and (ii) phase diagrams showing regions in $(u_{D},\delta,\mu)$ where Berry-curvature-dipole or quantum-metric-dipole contributions are large. A practical diagnostic is identified: in a valley-polarized setting where the threefold rotation symmetry $C_{3z}$ is preserved but time-reversal symmetry $\mathcal{T}$ is broken, with an applied electric field $E_y$ along the $y$-direction, the low-temperature nonlinear Hall conductivity $\sigma_{xy}(E_y) \equiv j_1^x(E_y)/E_y$ obeys $\sigma_{xy}(E_y)=L_{1,1}^{x,y}+L_{1,11}^{x,yy}E_y$, where $L_{1,1}^{x,y}$ is the linear charge conductivity coefficient controlled by the net Berry curvature, and $L_{1,11}^{x,yy}$ is the second-order charge conductivity coefficient controlled by the quantum-metric dipole $\int_{k} f_{0}\partial_{k_{x}}G^{yy}$, with $f_0$ the equilibrium Fermi-Dirac distribution and $G^{yy}$ the $yy$ component of the quantum metric. These numerical results identify Bernal bilayer graphene near band extrema as a gate-tunable platform for testing the generalized nonlinear Wiedemann–Franz/Mott relations and for isolating quantum-metric effects.

Describe the practical diagnostic proposed and its basis in symmetry and the model calculations: in a valley-polarized, $C_{3z}$-symmetric but time-reversal-broken setting (so that net Berry curvature can be nonzero at linear order), apply an electric field $E_{y}$ and measure the low-temperature nonlinear Hall conductivity defined as $\\sigma_{xy}(E_{y})\\equiv j_{1}^{x}(E_{y})/E_{y}$.
